title: WHY DID JESUS ASK PETER THREE TIMES, “DO YOU LOVE ME?”
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS ASK PETER THREE TIMES, “DO YOU LOVE ME?”

Peter denied Jesus three times. Then, beside another charcoal fire, the risen Christ asked him a question three times—not to destroy the man who failed Him, but to restore him where his shame still remembered everything.
There are failures you confess to God…
and then there are failures that keep talking to you after you have already confessed them.
Peter knew the difference.

He had watched Jesus heal the sick. He had seen demons flee. He had walked on water toward Christ. He had stood on a mountain and witnessed a glimpse of His glory. When Jesus asked His disciples who they believed He was, Peter had answered:
“You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”
Peter was not merely interested in Jesus.
He loved Him.
And yet, on the night when loyalty became dangerous, Peter collapsed.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
That number matters.
Because after the resurrection, Jesus would meet Peter beside a fire and ask him something three times.
“Do you love Me?”
But to understand why that question could have pierced Peter so deeply, we have to return to another fire.
A few days earlier, Jesus had been arrested.
Peter followed at a distance.
John tells us something strangely specific about the place where Peter stood:
“Now the servants and officers had made a charcoal fire…”
The Greek word is ἀνθρακιά—anthrakia.
A charcoal fire.
John 18:18.
There Peter warmed himself while Jesus was being interrogated.
Then the questions started.
“You are not also one of this Man’s disciples, are you?”
Peter answered:
“I am not.”
The man who once declared that Jesus was the Christ now denied even belonging to Him.
Another accusation came.
Another denial.
Then another.
Three denials.
And Luke records one of the most devastating details in the entire Passion narrative.
After Peter’s third denial, the rooster crowed.
“And the Lord turned and looked at Peter.”
Imagine that moment.
Jesus did not need witnesses.
Peter knew.
Jesus knew.
Their eyes met.
Then Peter remembered what Jesus had told him.
Before the rooster crowed, Peter would deny Him three times.
Luke says Peter went outside and wept bitterly.
Those were not the tears of a man who had merely made an embarrassing mistake.
Those were the tears of a man discovering that he was not as strong as he thought he was.
Maybe that is why Peter’s story feels so painfully familiar.
Some of us have never denied Jesus beside a literal fire.
But we have denied Him with our choices.
We confessed Christ on Sunday and compromised by Monday.
We promised God we were finished with that sin…
and returned to it.
We told Jesus, “I’ll never do that again.”
Then we did.
We worshiped while carrying something hidden.
We quoted Scripture while privately losing battles nobody knew existed.
We looked strong enough to encourage everybody else while wondering whether God was disappointed every time He looked at us.
And perhaps the hardest part of failure is not simply remembering what you did.
It is remembering who you thought you were before you did it.
Peter had said:
“Even if all are made to stumble because of You, I will never be made to stumble.”
He was certain.
Then came the courtyard.
The questions.
The fear.
The fire.
The rooster.
The look.
And Peter broke.
But the Gospel did not end beside Peter’s failure.
Jesus was crucified.
Jesus died.
Jesus was buried.
And on the third day, Jesus Christ rose bodily from the dead.
Sin had not defeated Him.
Death had not held Him.
The grave had not kept Him.
And after the resurrection, John 21 brings us to another morning.
Peter and several disciples had been fishing through the night and caught nothing.
At daybreak, someone stood on the shore.
It was Jesus.
At His command they cast the net again, and suddenly it filled with fish.
John recognized Him.
“It is the Lord!”
Peter did what Peter does.
He threw himself into the sea to get to Jesus.
And when he reached the shore, something was waiting.
John 21:9 says:
“Then, as soon as they had come to land, they saw a fire of coals there…”
There it is again.
ἀνθρακιά.
Anthrakia.
A charcoal fire.
Remarkably, this Greek noun occurs only twice in the New Testament.
John 18.
John 21.
One charcoal fire stood near Peter’s denial.
The other stood near Peter’s restoration.
Do not rush past that.
Jesus could have met Peter anywhere.
But John deliberately places another charcoal fire in the story.
Imagine what Peter might have remembered as he smelled the smoke.
The courtyard.
The questions.
The denial.
The rooster.
His own voice saying, “I am not.”
Now the risen Jesus is sitting near another fire.
And He feeds Peter breakfast.
That detail is breathtaking.
Before Jesus confronts Peter’s failure, He feeds him.
There is fish.
There is bread.
There is a fire.
There is Jesus.
Peter is sitting across from the One he denied…
and Christ has not abandoned him.
Then breakfast ends.
Jesus turns toward Peter.
“Simon, son of Jonah, do you love Me more than these?”
In Greek:
Σίμων Ἰωάννου, ἀγαπᾷς με πλέον τούτων;
Simōn Iōannou, agapas me pleon toutōn?
“Simon, son of John, do you love Me more than these?”
Peter responds:
Ναί, κύριε, σὺ οἶδας ὅτι φιλῶ σε.
Nai, kyrie, sy oidas hoti philō se.
“Yes, Lord; You know that I love You.”
Jesus answers:
Βόσκε τὰ ἀρνία μου.
Boske ta arnia mou.
“Feed My lambs.”
Then Jesus asks again.
“Simon, son of John, do you love Me?”
Peter answers again.
“Yes, Lord; You know that I love You.”
Jesus tells him:
“Tend My sheep.”
Then comes the third time.
“Simon, son of John, do you love Me?”
And John tells us:
Peter was grieved because He said to him the third time, “Do you love Me?”
That sentence unlocks the emotional center of the scene.
Three times.
Not because Jesus had forgotten Peter’s first answer.
Not because the risen Son of God needed reassurance.
Peter had denied Jesus three times.
Now Christ gives Peter three opportunities to confess his love.
Denial had spoken three times.
Now love would speak three times.
Failure had repeated itself.
Now restoration would answer it.
This does not mean Peter purchased forgiveness by saying “I love You” three times. The Gospel never teaches that sinners earn grace through emotional performance.
Grace comes from Christ.
Forgiveness rests on what Jesus accomplished through His death and resurrection.
Peter was not negotiating his way back into the love of God.
He was being restored by the Lord he had denied.
And there is another detail Christians sometimes hear explained in a way that deserves care.
In the first two questions John records Jesus using the verb ἀγαπάω—agapaō—while Peter responds with φιλέω—phileō. In the third question, Jesus uses phileō as well.

Some sermons build the entire passage around the claim that these words necessarily represent two sharply different levels of love—as though Jesus first asks for divine, superior love while Peter can offer only a lesser friendship-love.
That interpretation can preach beautifully.
But we should not force the Greek beyond what the context securely proves.

John frequently varies near-synonymous Greek words stylistically. In this very passage he also varies words associated with tending, feeding, sheep, and lambs. Many scholars therefore caution against constructing the meaning of the entire encounter upon a rigid distinction between agapaō and phileō.
The unmistakable emphasis supplied by the text itself is simpler and more devastating:
Jesus asked three times.
Peter had denied three times.
And by the third question, Peter was grieved.
Jesus was touching the wound.
But He was not touching it to torture Peter.
He was touching it to restore him.
There is a difference between condemnation and conviction.
Condemnation tells you to run away from Christ because you failed.
Grace brings you back to Christ because He alone can save and restore you.
Jesus did not pretend Peter’s denial never happened.
Grace is not amnesia.
Jesus brought Peter to the place where love had to answer what fear had done.
And every time Peter answered, Jesus gave him responsibility.
“Feed My lambs.”
“Tend My sheep.”
“Feed My sheep.”
Think about that.
Jesus was not merely saying:
“I forgive you.”
He was effectively showing Peter:
“I still have work for you.”
The man who failed publicly was not discarded permanently.
The disciple who broke under pressure was not thrown into heaven’s garbage pile.
Jesus restored him to service.
But notice whose sheep they were.
“My lambs.”
“My sheep.”
The church would never belong to Peter.
The people would belong to Jesus.
Peter was being entrusted with caring for people Christ Himself had purchased.
That is grace with responsibility.
Forgiveness does not make sin insignificant.
Grace transforms forgiven sinners into people who belong to Christ and are called to follow Him.
And Jesus was not finished.
After restoring Peter, Christ told him that one day following Him would cost Peter dearly.
Then came the words Peter had first heard years before:
“Follow Me.”
Imagine hearing those words after everything.
Follow Me.
After the denial?
Follow Me.
After the cowardice?
Follow Me.
After breaking the promise?
Follow Me.
After discovering how weak I really am?
Follow Me.
Peter’s story did not end with a rooster crowing.
It continued with the voice of Jesus calling.
Maybe yours can too.
Perhaps you are reading this with your own charcoal fire burning somewhere in your memory.
A marriage you damaged.
A secret addiction.
A season of compromise.
A lie nobody discovered.
A relationship you knew dishonored God.
A faith you slowly abandoned.
A promise to God you repeatedly broke.
A hidden habit you have become frighteningly good at concealing.
Maybe people still think you are strong.
But you remember the courtyard.
You remember what happened when pressure came.
You remember the version of yourself you wish nobody had ever met.
Listen carefully.
Peter’s restoration does not mean everybody automatically receives Peter’s particular apostolic calling, nor does it mean repentance has no consequences.
It means something far better.
Your failure does not possess greater saving power than the blood of Jesus Christ.
Your worst chapter is not stronger than the cross.
Your shame is not lord.
Your past is not savior.
Jesus is.
Scripture says:
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not because sin is small.
Because Christ is sufficient.
At the cross, Jesus bore sin.
He endured judgment.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the answer to human scandal is not self-improvement.
It is the Gospel.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Stop defending what Christ died to forgive.
Stop calling bondage “just who I am.”
Stop hiding behind religious appearances.
Bring the truth to Jesus.
Peter could not rewrite the courtyard.
Neither can you rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus Christ can redeem what yesterday did to you and transform what tomorrow becomes.
That is the difference between scandal and grace.
Scandal says, “Look what Peter did.”
Grace says, “Look what Jesus did with Peter.”
Scandal freezes a human being at the worst moment of his life.
Grace refuses to pretend the moment never happened—but places that moment beneath the authority of the crucified and risen Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe the question reaching you today is not, “Have you ever failed?”
You already know that answer.
Maybe the question is:
Do you love Him?
Not, “Can you impress Him?”
Not, “Can you make everyone believe you have everything together?”
Not, “Can you erase your history?”
Do you love Jesus?
And if you do…
will you follow Him?
Will you repent where repentance is needed?
Will you forgive because you have been forgiven?
Will you leave the hidden thing?
Will you stop pretending?
Will you feed the people He puts in your care?
Will you let your failure make you humbler instead of harder?
Will you allow grace to become obedience?
Because biblical grace does not merely make us feel better about yesterday.
Grace trains us to belong to Jesus today.
Talk to Christ.
And if you need to say it somewhere, say it here:
Not because typing those words saves you.
Only Jesus saves.
But sometimes honesty begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
And if you are still fighting for your faith after failure, comment, “I’m still following Jesus.”
Someone else reading the comments may desperately need to discover that Christians are not people who never fall.
We are people whose only hope is the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
Not for an algorithm.
For a person.

There may be someone quietly drowning in shame who would never tell you what they have done, but they may read something you share at two in the morning and realize that Peter’s failure was not the end of Peter.
Send this to the believer who thinks Jesus has finished with them.
Supporting Gospel work should never be treated as a payment to God, a way to purchase His favor, or proof that someone is saved.
Invite your family.
Send it to the person who has stopped going to church.
Send it to the Christian who fell.
Send it to the seeker who thinks Christianity is only for people with clean histories.
Even send it to the unbelieving friend who believes their past has made them unreachable.
Because the Gospel was never the announcement that good people can save themselves.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Peter once stood beside a charcoal fire and said:
“I am not.”
Later, beside another charcoal fire, Jesus looked at that same broken disciple and called him forward again.
That may be the line you need to carry with you tonight:
The fire that remembers your failure does not get the final word when the risen Jesus is standing beside it.
